title: One Divides Another
statement: What is the smallest $n$ such that every $n$-element subset of $\{1,2,\dots,100\}$ contains two distinct numbers, one of which divides the other?
insight: Write each number as 2^k·m with m odd: there are 50 odd parts, and numbers sharing an odd part form a divisibility chain (pigeonhole). {51,…,100} shows 50 is not enough.
redHerring: Building large sets greedily and trying to prove they're maximal by hand.
hints: First find a large set with no divisibility pairs. Try the top half.
Every number is $2^k m$ with $m$ odd. How many possible $m$ are there?
Two numbers with the same odd part: does one divide the other?
solution:
Lower bound: $\{51,\dots,100\}$ has 50 elements and no divisibility pairs (twice the smallest is already over 100). So $n \ge 51$.

Upper bound: write each number as $2^k m$ with $m$ odd, $m\in\{1,3,\dots,99\}$: 50 possibilities. Among 51 numbers, two share an odd part by pigeonhole, and then the smaller divides the larger. So $n = 51$.
